newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Schiphol names cargo carriers hit by noise rules.
newsitem.headline: Schiphol names cargo carriers hit by noise rules.

text.p: Eight freight airlines will be hit by Amsterdam Schiphol airport's latest move to tighten its regulations concerning noisy (Chapter Two) aircraft.

A spokeswoman from Schiphol airport said the eight carriers in question are Affretair, Polar Air Cargo, Trans Mediterranean Airways and charter operators: African International Airways, Liberia World Airlines, DAS Air Cargo, Simba Air Cargo and M.K.Air Cargo.

The Dutch airport will further tighten its noise regulations from April 1. This has already had an impact on the cargo carriers. Nigerian carrier, M.K.Air Cargo has decided to stop operating to the airport and Simba, a Kenyan airline, is expected to stop operations to Schiphol after the April deadline, said the spokeswoman.

Chapter Two aircraft are currently forbidden to land and take-off between 2300-0600 local(2100-0400gmt) but from April this will be extended from 1800-0800 local(1600-0800gmt) the airport authority said.
At the same time:"Airlines will have to pay 100 percent more in charges, if they continue to use Chapter Two engined-aircraft.
For take-off weights of up to 100 tonnes, the charges will be 1,200 guilders and for above 100 tonnes, they will be 1,800 guilders.

"For instance, for aircraft with up to 100 tonnes take-off weight. will be charged an unchanged halding fee of 830 guilders from April 1, plus a doubled Chapter Two user fee of 1,200 guilders. For aircraft of over 100 tonnes take-off weight the landing fee is 1,800 guilders and the the Chapter Two is also 1,800 guilders."

However airines can get some money back if they enter into a contract with the airport authority which sets out their plans for quieter (Chapter Three) aircraft. Carriers have to say whether they intend to renew their fleet and eventually phase out their Chapter Two aircraft, the airport authority said.
Around 22 airlines have so-far signed these contracts.

The airport could not say whether any of the freight carriers will leave the airport due to the tougher regulations. "They are still thinking about it. We may lose traffic but we have no choice," said the spokeswoman.
In 1996, 10 percent of Schiphol's traffic were Chapter Two flights but the airport authority aims to reduce the number of these flights to less than seven percent this year.

Even though the Ilyushin 76 and Tupolev 154M are not classed as Chapter Two aircraft, they will also be affected by the new regulations. Boeing 747-100 aircraft with Pratt & Whitney JT9D-7 engines will also be hit by these new rules.

Schiphol increased its charges for Chapter Two aircraft by 100 percent in November last year. Aircraft with a payload of up to 100 tons were charged 600 guilders and 900 guilders the payload was above 100 tons. --Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44-171-542-7706 Fax+5017
